## Kotlin Multiplatform vs React Native for Business Apps
URL: https://appvionstudio.com/insights/kotlin-multiplatform-vs-react-native/
======================================================================

Choosing a framework
### Kotlin Multiplatform vs React Native for business apps.
By Ayyaz Sajjad, Founder & CEO · Published 22 Sep 2026 · Updated 22 Oct 2026
Most comparisons of these two frameworks are written by people who sell one of them. This one is written by a studio that builds Kotlin Multiplatform products and has shipped against React Native teams. The honest summary is that they share different things, and the right answer depends on one question about your product rather than on which framework is newer.
The short answer
#### React Native shares the interface. Kotlin Multiplatform shares the logic.
That single sentence explains almost every practical difference between them, including cost, hiring, performance and the kind of bug you will spend your evenings on.
React Native shares
All screens and components
Navigation and layout
Business rules and validation
Networking and state
One JavaScript or TypeScript codebase
Kotlin Multiplatform shares
Domain models and business rules
Validation and use cases
Networking and API contracts
Local database, caching and sync
Nothing in the interface, deliberately
What that costs you
React Native gives you one interface to build and one to maintain, which is genuinely fast. The price is that your screens are written in JavaScript and React Native turns them into native views at runtime, so every native capability arrives through a library someone else maintains.
Kotlin Multiplatform gives you two interfaces to build. The price is real. What you get back is that the interface is the platform’s own, and the rules that decide whether an invoice is correct exist exactly once.
Where each one breaks
#### The failure modes nobody puts in the pitch deck.
Both frameworks work. Both have a characteristic way of going wrong, and knowing which one you can live with matters more than any benchmark.
Where React Native struggles
Background work and offline sync, where each platform’s rules differ and the abstraction leaks
Heavy hardware use — continuous GPS, camera pipelines, Bluetooth — which usually ends in a native module anyway
Long lists of fast-changing data, which need careful tuning to stay smooth
Dependency risk: a critical library going unmaintained is your problem, not the framework’s
OS upgrades, where you wait for the ecosystem rather than for the platform
Where Kotlin Multiplatform struggles
First-version cost, because two interfaces are two interfaces
Hiring, if you want one developer to cover both platforms — you need Android and iOS skills
A smaller library ecosystem than JavaScript, though the gap has closed sharply
iOS tooling and debugging, which is better than it was but still rougher than Android
Teams that treat it as “write once” and then fight it when it is not
The honest version
If your app is mostly screens, forms and a server that does the thinking, React Native will get you there faster and cheaper, and the compromises may never bite.
If your app makes decisions on the device, works when the signal drops, or leans on hardware, Kotlin Multiplatform puts the difficult code in one place and leaves the platform to do what it is good at.
A decision rule
#### Four questions that settle it in ten minutes.
Question one
##### Does the app work offline?
Not “does it cache” — does a user complete real work with no signal, and does that work reconcile later? If yes, lean Kotlin Multiplatform. Offline-first means conflict rules, sync state and a local database, and those are exactly what you do not want written twice.
Question two
##### How expensive is a rule being wrong?
If a mis-calculated price, a missed approval or a wrong dispatch costs real money or safety, share the logic. If the worst case is a cosmetic bug, that pressure is absent and React Native is a reasonable call.
Question three
##### Who maintains it in two years?
A React team that will own this app forever is a strong argument for React Native. A team that will hand it to mobile engineers, or no in-house team at all, is an argument for the platform’s own languages, where hiring is easier and knowledge is not framework-specific.
Question four
##### Do you actually need iOS on day one?
Many operational apps are Android-only for years, because the field hardware is Android. If that is you, the comparison dissolves: build native Android now and structure it so the domain layer can move into a shared module later, without a rewrite.
What we use, and why
#### We build Kotlin Multiplatform, and we will tell you when not to.
Our work is operational: dispatch, approvals, attendance, proof of delivery, field service. That category answers question one and question two the same way almost every time — the app must work without signal, and a wrong record is expensive. So the shared-logic model fits, and that is why we build the way we do.
D. Delivery is a three-app Kotlin Multiplatform logistics platform with realtime dispatch, payments and offline-first sync — the clearest example of why the line sits where it does. PropFix applies the same structure to property maintenance and field work orders.
If you describe your product and it turns out React Native is the right tool for it, you will get that answer straight. It is a cheaper thing to hear now than in month five. Our pricing page publishes real numbers, including what a clarity sprint costs if you want the decision documented before committing to a build.
FAQ
#### Questions people ask before choosing.
Is Kotlin Multiplatform better than React Native?
Neither is better in general, and anyone who says otherwise is selling something. They share different things. React Native shares the user interface and renders it itself, which is fastest when the app is mostly screens and forms and one team owns both platforms. Kotlin Multiplatform shares the business logic and keeps each interface genuinely native, which wins when correctness matters, when the app is offline-first, or when it uses hardware heavily.
Is Kotlin Multiplatform production ready in 2026?
Yes. Kotlin Multiplatform has been stable since November 2023, and Google officially supports it for sharing business logic between Android and iOS. It runs in production at large engineering organisations, and at smaller studios shipping multi-role operational platforms with realtime dispatch, payments and offline sync.
Which is cheaper to build?
React Native is usually cheaper for a first version, because one team writes one interface. Kotlin Multiplatform is usually cheaper across a two to three year life, because the rules that cause expensive bugs exist once rather than twice, and you do not accumulate a backlog of platform workarounds in the interface layer. If the app will be rewritten in eighteen months either way, that long-run argument does not apply and you should take the cheaper first version.
Can we migrate an existing React Native app to Kotlin Multiplatform?
Yes, but not incrementally in the way an Android-to-KMP migration can be. A React Native app shares its interface, so moving to KMP means rewriting the interface natively on each platform while the business rules move into a shared Kotlin module. Plan it as a rebuild that reuses your backend, not as a refactor, and be honest about whether the reason justifies it.
Does Kotlin Multiplatform work for iOS?
Yes. The shared Kotlin module compiles to a native framework that Swift and SwiftUI consume like any other dependency. The iOS interface is written in Swift, so it behaves like a native iOS app rather than a port. This is the part people find surprising: KMP does not put a Kotlin interface on iOS, and is not trying to.
What about Flutter?
Flutter sits on the same side of the line as React Native: it shares the interface. Unlike React Native, it does not use the platform’s own views; it draws every control itself with its own rendering engine. Every native capability still arrives through a plugin, and the four questions above apply to Flutter unchanged.
Start the conversation
#### Not sure which side of the line your product sits on?
Bring the product, the platforms you need, and the constraints. Twenty minutes is usually enough to answer the four questions above — and if the answer is that you do not need us, you will get that straight.

Real prices
### How much does a Kotlin Multiplatform app cost?
By Ayyaz Sajjad, Founder & CEO · Published 22 Oct 2026
A production Kotlin Multiplatform app built by AppVion Studio costs $12,000 to $35,000. A focused first release on Android and iOS lands at $12,000 to $18,000 over 8 to 12 weeks; a multi-role operational platform runs $20,000 to $35,000 over 12 to 16 weeks. These are our published prices. This page explains what moves a project inside that range, and what sits outside it.

Where the saving comes from
#### Adding iOS adds 35 to 55 percent, not 100.
Kotlin Multiplatform shares the expensive part of an app, the rules, once. On a $12,000 Android-only scope, adding iOS this way typically adds about $4,200 to $6,600, not another $12,000.
##### Written once, in Kotlin
Domain models and business rules, validation, networking and API contracts, the local database and the offline sync logic.
##### Built for each platform
The interface, navigation, permissions and system dialogs, camera and location, push notifications and secure credential storage.
##### The optional extra saving
Compose Multiplatform can share the screens too, which cuts interface work further. The trade is an interface that follows each platform's conventions a little less closely.
What moves the number
#### Seven things decide almost every quote.
Screen count is the weakest predictor of cost. These are the strongest.
##### Number of user roles
One role is a list and a detail screen. Four roles with different permissions is four products sharing a backend. This is the biggest driver on operational apps.
##### Whether the data is live
Pull-to-refresh is cheap. Screens that update the moment a driver moves need realtime infrastructure, conflict handling and much more testing.
##### Offline behaviour
Working offline means a local database, a sync queue and a decision about conflicting edits. In Kotlin Multiplatform that logic is written once for both platforms. How offline-first works.
##### Integrations
Payments, maps, SMS, calendars and existing ERP or CRM systems each bring their own edge cases. Three integrations often cost more than ten screens.
##### Interface ambition
Motion, empty states, loading and error states: the hundred small decisions that make an app feel expensive.
##### Platform count
Android only is the baseline. iOS through Kotlin Multiplatform adds 35 to 55 percent.
##### Scope clarity on day one
The most expensive projects are the ones that changed direction in week six. That is why the Clarity Sprint exists.
Costs outside the quote
#### What you pay directly, in your own name.
Third-party accounts are always registered to you, so nothing has to be transferred or can be withheld if the working relationship ends.

Already on Android?

If your Android app is written in Kotlin with its rules kept out of the screens, the domain and data layers move into a shared module while the Android app keeps shipping. How cleanly it is layered today decides the price, and the Clarity Sprint measures exactly that.

FAQ
#### Questions people ask first.
How much does a Kotlin Multiplatform app cost?
At AppVion Studio a production Kotlin Multiplatform app costs $12,000 to $35,000. A focused first release lands at $12,000 to $18,000 over 8 to 12 weeks; a multi-role operational platform with dispatch, approvals, live tracking or payments runs $20,000 to $35,000 over 12 to 16 weeks.
Is Kotlin Multiplatform cheaper than building two native apps?
Usually, yes. Adding iOS through Kotlin Multiplatform typically adds 35 to 55 percent to an Android-only build rather than doubling it, because the business logic, networking and local database are written once and only the interface is built per platform.
Is Kotlin Multiplatform cheaper than Flutter?
For an interface-heavy app with little logic, Flutter is usually cheaper to start. For an operational app where a wrong rule costs money, Kotlin Multiplatform tends to cost less over the life of the product, because rules are written and fixed once. See Kotlin Multiplatform vs Flutter.
What is not included in the price?
Third-party costs that belong to you and are paid directly: the Apple Developer Program at $99 a year, Google Play Console at a one-off $25, and hosting, database, mapping, SMS or payment fees. Maintenance after launch is a separate retainer from $900 a month.
Why start with a Clarity Sprint?
Because the most expensive projects are the ones that change direction halfway through. The sprint, from $1,500 over one to two weeks, fixes the scope, the workflow map and the technical direction, including whether Kotlin Multiplatform is the right call at all, and ends in a fixed quote.

## Offline-First Mobile App Development: How It Works
URL: https://appvionstudio.com/insights/offline-first-mobile-app-development/
======================================================================

Engineering for the field
### Offline-first mobile app development: how it actually works.
By Ayyaz Sajjad, Founder & CEO · Published 22 Oct 2026
An offline-first app treats the database on the phone as the place work is recorded, and the server as the place it is shared. Every action is saved on the device first and synced when a connection exists, so a rider in a basement or a teacher in a thick-walled lecture hall never waits on a spinner. This is how we build it, from apps we have shipped.
Book a free 20-min call See an offline-first build
The short answer
#### Offline-first and offline-friendly are not the same thing.
Most apps that claim to work offline only keep old data readable. Offline-first means new work can be recorded with no signal at all. Android's own offline-first guide puts it the same way: the app performs all, or a critical part, of its core work without the internet.
Offline-friendly vs offline-first mobile apps
Behaviour
Offline-friendly
Offline-first
Reading data with no signal
Yes, what was already downloaded
Yes
Recording new work with no signal
No, it waits or fails
Yes, synced later
Where the truth lives
On the server
On the phone first, then the server
Good for
News, announcements, catalogues
Deliveries, inspections, attendance, field jobs
Our example
WUM Connect announcements
D. Delivery rider app, Attendance Management
How it is built
#### Five parts every offline-first app needs.
##### 1. A local database as the source of truth
Screens read from the database on the phone, never straight from the network. We use SQLDelight in Kotlin Multiplatform and Room on Android, encrypted with SQLCipher when the data is sensitive.
##### 2. An outbox for every change
Each action is written as a queued change on the device. In D. Delivery every step of a job goes through a local outbox in an encrypted on-device database.
##### 3. A background sync worker
A worker drains the outbox when the connection returns, even if the app is closed. In Attendance Management a WorkManager job does this, so a register is never lost.
##### 4. Conflict rules the server enforces
Decide what happens when two people change the same record, and let the server have the final word on money and status. A modified phone cannot skip a step the server forbids.
##### 5. Sync status the user can see
PropFix tells a worker the difference between "nothing to do" and "we have not heard from the server lately", a distinction most apps quietly collapse.
##### Plus: media that waits its turn
Photos and videos are compressed on the phone before upload and queued in the background, so a weak signal never stops someone finishing a job.
Conflicts
#### Three ways to settle a conflicting edit.
There is no universal answer. The right rule depends on what the record is and what a wrong value costs.
##### Last write wins
The most recent change replaces the older one. Simple and fine for personal settings or notes. Wrong for anything two people depend on.
##### The server decides
The phone proposes, the server checks the rules and accepts or rejects. Right for order status, payments and anything a business is paid on.
##### Append-only
Records are never edited in place; each change is added as a new entry. Our attendance platform keeps an append-only audit log, so a disputed record has a history.
Cost and platform
#### Offline is not a toggle, so plan it from day one.
Offline behaviour is one of the seven things that move an app's price on our pricing page. It is far cheaper to design in from the start than to bolt onto an app that assumed a connection. The sync rules are logic, so with Kotlin Multiplatform they are written once and behave the same on Android and iOS.
Data-heavy utility
##### Attendance Management
Mark now, sync later: offline capture, background sync and an append-only audit log across four roles.
Read the case study
Logistics platform
##### D. Delivery
An encrypted local outbox for every job step, with video proof uploads queued on weak signal.
Read the case study
Field service
##### PropFix
Work orders with a sync status the contractor can see, from one shared Kotlin core.
Read the case study
FAQ
#### Questions people ask first.
What is an offline-first app?
An offline-first app records every action in a database on the phone first and syncs it with the server when a connection exists. Reading and writing both work with no signal, so the user never waits for the network and never loses work because of it.
What is the difference between offline-first and offline-friendly?
An offline-friendly app keeps what it has already downloaded readable without signal, but needs a connection to record anything new. An offline-first app also records new work offline and syncs it later. Field and operational apps usually need the second.
How does an offline app handle two people editing the same record?
With a rule decided at design time. Common choices are last write wins for personal data, server decides for anything involving money or status, and append-only records where nothing is edited in place. The server should enforce the rules that matter, because a phone can be modified.
Does offline-first cost more?
Yes. It needs a local database, a sync queue, conflict rules and a lot more testing, so it is one of the seven things that move an app's price. It costs far less to design in from the start than to add to an app built online-only.
Can an existing app be made offline-first?
Usually, if its data layer is separate from its screens. Writes are routed through a local outbox and a sync worker is added. How much has to change first is what a Clarity Sprint establishes.
Start the conversation
#### Building something that has to work without a network?
Attendance, inspections, deliveries, stock counts: if work happens away from a desk, twenty minutes is enough to map what has to work offline and what can wait.
Book a free 20-min call WhatsApp us

## Kotlin Multiplatform vs Flutter for Business Apps
URL: https://appvionstudio.com/insights/kotlin-multiplatform-vs-flutter/
======================================================================

Choosing a framework
### Kotlin Multiplatform vs Flutter for business apps.
By Ayyaz Sajjad, Founder & CEO · Published 21 Oct 2026 · Updated 22 Oct 2026
Both let one team ship Android and iOS. They get there in opposite ways, and for an operational business app that difference decides cost, risk and how the app feels to the people who use it every day. This is the comparison from a studio that builds Kotlin Multiplatform and will say when Flutter is the better call.
Book a free 20-min call Read KMP vs React Native
The short answer
#### Flutter shares the interface and draws it itself. Kotlin Multiplatform shares the logic.
Flutter apps are written in Dart and render every pixel with Flutter's own engine. Kotlin Multiplatform shares business logic in Kotlin and, by default, lets each platform draw its own native interface.
##### Flutter shares
All screens and widgets, navigation, business rules and networking, in one Dart codebase drawn by Flutter's rendering engine on every platform.
##### Kotlin Multiplatform shares
Domain models, business rules, validation, networking and the local database in Kotlin. Screens can stay native, or be shared with Compose Multiplatform when that is the better trade.
##### What that means for you
Flutter gives one interface to build and maintain. Kotlin Multiplatform gives one set of rules that cannot drift between Android and iOS, with interfaces that follow each platform's own conventions.
Where each one breaks
#### The failure modes to plan for.
##### Flutter: the platform is imitated
Flutter redraws native controls rather than using them, so platform conventions, accessibility behaviour and new OS features arrive when the framework catches up.
##### Flutter: a separate language
Dart is used almost only for Flutter. Native Android and iOS knowledge still matters for anything below the interface, through plugins and platform channels.
##### KMP: more interface work if you keep it native
Sharing only the logic means building two interfaces. That is the price of a fully native feel; Compose Multiplatform removes it when a shared interface is acceptable.
##### KMP: two build systems
iOS builds go through Xcode and Gradle together. It is well supported, but the team needs someone comfortable on both sides.
Choosing in ten minutes
#### Four questions that settle it.
##### Where does the value sit?
Mostly in screens and content: Flutter. Mostly in rules, money, state and sync: Kotlin Multiplatform.
##### Do you already have a Kotlin Android app?
Then Kotlin Multiplatform extends it. Flutter replaces it.
##### How native must it feel?
Field teams, accessibility needs and heavy use of the camera, location or background work favour native interfaces.
##### Does it work offline?
Offline-first data and sync rules are logic. Writing them once in Kotlin is where KMP pays back most. How offline-first works.
Our position
#### We build Kotlin Multiplatform, and we will tell you when not to.
Our operational products, like D. Delivery and PropFix, run on shared Kotlin because their value is in rules that must not drift: dispatch, proof of work, payments. For a content-led app with little logic and one design for both platforms, Flutter is a reasonable choice and we will say so in the first call.
Kotlin Multiplatform
##### Our KMP service
How we split shared logic from native interfaces, the stack we use, and what a project costs.
See the service
Comparison
##### KMP vs React Native
The same question against React Native: what each shares and where each one breaks.
Read the article
Pricing
##### What an app costs
Published prices for the Clarity Sprint and full builds.
See pricing
FAQ
#### Questions people ask first.
Is Kotlin Multiplatform better than Flutter?
Neither is better in general. Flutter is faster when the product is mostly screens and one shared interface is the goal. Kotlin Multiplatform is the stronger choice when the value sits in business rules, offline data and platform behaviour that must stay native.
Can Kotlin Multiplatform share the interface like Flutter?
Yes, if you want it to. Compose Multiplatform lets a KMP project share screens across Android and iOS. The difference is that it is optional: you can share only the logic and keep a native interface where it matters.
Which is cheaper to build?
For an interface-heavy app with little logic, Flutter is usually cheaper to start. For an operational app where a wrong rule costs money, sharing the logic with Kotlin Multiplatform tends to cost less over the life of the product, because rules are written and fixed once.
We already have an Android app. Which should we choose?
If it is written in Kotlin, Kotlin Multiplatform is the natural next step: the domain and data layers can move into a shared module while the Android app keeps working. Moving to Flutter means rewriting the app in Dart. See moving an Android app to Kotlin Multiplatform.
Start the conversation
#### Not sure which side of the line your product sits on?
Twenty minutes is usually enough to tell. We will give you a straight recommendation, even if it is not Kotlin Multiplatform.

## SnowGrid Case Study: Fleet Dispatch App | AppVion Studio
URL: https://appvionstudio.com/work/snowgrid/
======================================================================

Fleet dispatch & field service
### SnowGrid: a three-role dispatch platform for snow removal operations.
One platform serving three completely different jobs — an operator running the fleet, a property owner buying a service, and a contractor working in the field in bad weather. Live dispatch mapping, map-based area measurement, photo verification, and Stripe escrow payments.
Fleet management Real-time dispatch GPS tracking Stripe payments Multi-role platform
3 user roles 14 screens Live GPS dispatch
Published 16 Aug 2026 · Updated 21 Oct 2026
Get it on Google Play Explore the Interactive Demo Build something like this
The problem
#### Snow work is priced by guesswork and paid on trust.
Context
Snow removal is a weather-driven business. Demand arrives in unpredictable bursts, the work has to be dispatched within hours, and the size of a job depends on a physical area nobody has actually measured.
What kept breaking
Quotes were eyeballed, so margin varied wildly between jobs. Dispatch happened over the phone with no view of who was closest or already busy. And once the snow melted, there was no way to prove a property had actually been cleared — which made every disputed invoice a stalemate.
The real requirement
Three separate products that stay in sync: an operator command centre, a self-serve customer app, and a field-first contractor app — all reading and writing the same job state in real time.
The approach
#### One platform, three deliberately different products.
Each role got an interface designed around its actual working conditions, not a shared screen with features hidden by permission flags. The contractor app in particular is built for gloved hands, cold weather, and one-handed use in a vehicle.
01
##### Admin command centre
Seven screens for fleet management, live dispatch, revenue and escrow monitoring, pricing configuration, and oversight of every job in the system.
02
##### Customer app
Four screens: register a property, pin and measure its area on a live satellite map, choose snow depth and priority, get an instant quote, authorise payment.
03
##### Contractor app
Three screens: receive real-time assignments, toggle availability, submit before and after photo verification, handle disputes, and track earnings and payouts.
04
##### Shared services
Role-based authentication, a dynamic pricing engine, live GPS streaming, and Stripe escrow holding funds until work is verified.
Inside the apps
#### Screens from the shipped build.
Real screenshots from the three role-specific apps — the operator command centre, the customer booking flow, and the field contractor portal.
Measure the propertyCustomer · Map polygon tool
Request snow removalCustomer · A few taps
Pricing engineSnow company · Its own rates
Contractor payoutsContractor · Every job and what is owed
Three rolesOne app for office, crews and customers
Plans and billingSnow company · Usage against the plan
Engineering highlights
#### The parts that were harder than they look.
Map-based area measurement
Customers draw a polygon over their property on a satellite map and the system computes exact square footage from it. This is what turns a guessed quote into a calculated one — the single change with the largest effect on margin consistency across jobs.
Dynamic pricing engine
Price is a matrix, not a number: measured area combined with snow depth, priority tier, and environmental multipliers. Operators tune the matrix from the admin panel without a code change, so pricing can react to a season rather than waiting on a release.
Live dispatch map
Every active contractor streams position to a single operator map. Assignment decisions are made against who is genuinely nearest and available, rather than whoever picks up the phone first.
Escrow tied to proof
Payment is authorised up front and held in Stripe escrow. Before and after photos are the condition for release, which means the customer's protection and the contractor's payout depend on the same piece of evidence instead of on a phone call.
Scope at a glance
#### What the build actually covers.
03 Distinct user roles, each with a purpose-built interface rather than a shared screen.
14 Designed and built screens across the admin, customer, and contractor apps.
08 Core platform capabilities, from area measurement to escrow payout.
Live GPS fleet positions streamed to the operator dispatch map in real time.

## D. Delivery Case Study: KMP Logistics App | AppVion Studio
URL: https://appvionstudio.com/work/d-delivery/
======================================================================

Logistics & delivery platform
### D. Delivery: a Kotlin Multiplatform logistics platform built around verifiable proof of delivery.
Three connected products — a customer booking app, a rider job app, and an admin control tower — engineered so that every parcel movement leaves behind evidence that holds up in a dispute, and every rupee of cash-on-delivery is reconciled against the platform's own ledger rather than a rider's word.
Kotlin Multiplatform Jetpack Compose Supabase Realtime dispatch Proof of delivery
3 apps, 1 shared codebase 2 mandatory video proofs per delivery Customer app on Google Play
Published 16 Aug 2026 · Updated 23 Oct 2026
Get it on Google Play Build something like this See more work
The problem
#### Courier disputes are won by whoever has evidence — and nobody had any.
Context
The brief was a courier service for high-value goods in Pakistan — mobile phones, laptops, and electronics — where a single disputed parcel can cost more than a month of delivery revenue. The existing way of working was WhatsApp messages, phone calls, and a rider's memory.
What kept breaking
Nobody could prove what condition a device was in when it was collected. Cash collected on delivery was reconciled by hand and never quite matched. Riders were assigned by whoever answered first, not by who was actually closest. Customers called for status updates because there was nothing to look at.
The real requirement
Not "an app that books deliveries." A system where the evidence, the money, and the dispatch decision are all produced by the platform itself — so that the answer to "what happened to my parcel" is a record, not an argument.
The approach
#### One Kotlin Multiplatform codebase, three products, one source of truth.
Business logic, domain models, and data access live in a shared Kotlin module. The customer app and the rider app are native Jetpack Compose surfaces on top of it, and the admin control tower is a web panel against the same Postgres database. Shared logic means a pricing rule or an order-state rule is written once and cannot drift between apps. Why we chose this over a shared-UI framework is covered in Kotlin Multiplatform vs React Native for business apps.
01
##### Customer app
Category-aware booking, address search with a manual fallback, insurance based on declared value, live order tracking with a traffic-aware ETA, invoice and rating.
02
##### Rider app
Job broadcast, GPS foreground tracking, guided delivery steps, dual video capture, recipient e-signature, wallet and earnings ledger, offline-first sync.
03
##### Admin control tower
Manual dispatch, rider approval and document review, pricing configuration, dispute flags, and end-of-day cash settlement against the platform ledger.
04
##### Shared backend
Postgres with row-level security, realtime channels, storage for delivery evidence, edge functions for push dispatch, and scheduled jobs for the dispatch loop.
Interface design
#### The product design system the apps were built against.
The customer booking flow, IMEI capture, live tracking, and the rider's proof-of-delivery sequence.
IMEI CaptureCustomer · Scan or enter manually
Order PlacedCustomer · Booking confirmed
Live TrackingCustomer · ETA and pickup proof
Delivery ReceiptCustomer · IMEI and fare breakdown
Job AlertRider · Broadcast and dispatch
Video ProofRider · Pickup and drop-off
E-SignatureRider · Recipient confirms receipt
Rate DeliveryCustomer · Post-delivery feedback
Engineering highlights
#### The parts that were harder than they look.
Expanding-radius dispatch
A new order starts searching for riders inside a small radius and widens in steps on a scheduled server loop until someone accepts or the radius caps out and an admin is alerted. All loop state lives in the order row and is re-evaluated from scratch on every tick, so a missed notification or a dropped tick can never leave an order stuck in a phantom state.
Evidence pipeline
Pickup video, drop-off video, and a recipient e-signature are captured on-device, compressed before upload rather than after, and written to object storage under a per-order path. Uploads are queued through a background worker so a rider on a weak signal is never blocked from finishing a job.
Money integrity
Fares are computed on the server at order creation, not trusted from the client. Rider earnings are credited by a database trigger with a uniqueness guarantee, so a retried delivery confirmation can never pay twice. Cash owed back to the platform is calculated server-side and always nets out the rider's own commission — so the rider's figure and the admin's figure cannot disagree.
Server-enforced order states
The delivery lifecycle is a state machine enforced in the database, not just in the UI. A modified client cannot skip from "accepted" straight to "delivered" and bypass video capture, and a completed or cancelled order cannot be reopened.
Offline-first rider sync
Every job-progress mutation goes through a local outbox backed by an encrypted on-device database and is drained by a sync engine. A rider in a basement or a dead-zone keeps working; the server catches up when signal returns, and state is reconciled on resume rather than assumed.
Realtime that admits when it is unsure
Live subscriptions are treated as a latency optimisation, never as the only path for anything safety- or money-relevant. Each live screen is paired with a coarser reconciliation fetch on resume and on reconnect, so a dropped socket shows a reconnecting state instead of confidently stale data.
Scope at a glance
#### What the build actually covers.
03 Connected products delivered from one shared Kotlin Multiplatform codebase.
02 Mandatory video proofs per delivery, plus a recipient e-signature at drop-off.
13 Database tables placed under row-level security with per-role access policies.
100km Operational service radius, enforced on the client and again as a database constraint.
Technology
#### The stack behind D. Delivery.
Kotlin Multiplatform Jetpack Compose Coroutines & Flow Supabase Postgres Supabase Realtime Supabase Storage Row-Level Security Ktor Client SQLDelight SQLCipher Koin WorkManager CameraX ML Kit Firebase Cloud Messaging Firebase Crashlytics Google Maps & Places Google Routes API Edge Functions
Where it stands
#### The customer app is live on Google Play.
The customer and rider apps are functionally complete across booking, dispatch, tracking, proof capture, payments, wallet, and settlement. The platform has been through a structured security pass covering access control, fare tampering, rate limiting, input validation, encrypted session and database storage, and crash reporting. The customer app is published on Google Play; the rider app and the admin control tower run on the same shared Kotlin codebase.

## PropFix Case Study: Work Order App | AppVion Studio
URL: https://appvionstudio.com/work/profix/
======================================================================

Property maintenance platform
### PropFix: a field service command layer for modern maintenance teams.
A Kotlin Multiplatform maintenance workflow connecting property managers and the contractors who do the work — job assignment, proof of work, progress visibility, and manager approval in one system instead of four phone calls and a paper docket.
Kotlin Multiplatform Compose Multiplatform Supabase Work orders Multi-role
3 roles Android & iOS from one codebase Offline-capable
Published 16 Aug 2026 · Updated 21 Oct 2026
Watch the Demo Build something like this
The problem
#### Maintenance work is coordinated by whoever is willing to keep chasing it.
Context
A property manager looking after multiple sites is the hub of every maintenance job — taking the report, finding an available contractor, confirming the work happened, and answering for it if an owner asks later.
What kept breaking
Jobs lived in phone calls and messages, so nothing was searchable. Nobody could say which jobs were open right now without asking around. And "it's done" was a claim, not a record — which made invoice disputes unwinnable in either direction.
The real requirement
A shared state that all three parties read from and write to: the manager who raises the job, the contractor who does it, and the admin who oversees the whole portfolio.
Inside the app
#### Screens from the build.
Sign inRole-based entry, encrypted on device
TodayManager · The board at a glance
JobsManager · Open, dispatched, in progress
Job detailManager · Assign and evidence
My jobsContractor · What to do next
Your homeTenant · Report and follow up
The approach
#### Three roles, one shared job state.
01
##### Property manager
Raise a work order against a property, assign it to a contractor from the directory, and watch its status move without chasing anyone.
02
##### Contractor
Join by invite code, see assigned jobs, work through them, and attach proof of completion from the phone already in hand.
03
##### Admin
Oversee the full portfolio: every property, every contractor, every open job, plus billing and plan management.
04
##### Shared core
Domain models, repositories, and business rules live in shared Kotlin so Android and iOS cannot disagree about what a job's status means.
Engineering highlights
#### The parts that were harder than they look.
Invite-code onboarding
Contractors are not customers — they should not self-register into someone else's portfolio. Access is granted by a manager-generated invite code, so the contractor directory stays a curated list rather than an open sign-up form.
Proof of work
Before and after records attach to the job itself, not to a chat thread. When an invoice is queried months later, the evidence is already sitting on the record rather than somewhere in a phone's camera roll.
Sync you can see
The dashboard states its own sync status rather than silently assuming it is current. A field worker with poor signal can tell the difference between "nothing to do" and "we have not heard from the server lately" — a distinction most apps quietly collapse.
Shared logic, native shells
Compose Multiplatform with Koin dependency injection and a local SQLDelight cache. Business rules are written once; each platform keeps its own native presentation.

## GMassPulse Case Study: Email Outreach App | AppVion Studio
URL: https://appvionstudio.com/work/gmasspulse/
======================================================================

SaaS & automation platform
### GMassPulse: a mobile-first email outreach and campaign tracking platform.
Outreach tooling has always lived on the desktop. GMassPulse puts the whole loop — import a lead list, compose a personalised campaign, schedule follow-ups, and watch opens arrive in real time — on a phone, without shrinking a dashboard down to fit.
Email automation Google OAuth Supabase Live tracking Mobile-first SaaS
10 screens 4 core flows OAuth 2.0 secured
Published 16 Aug 2026 · Updated 21 Oct 2026
Explore the Interactive Demo Build something like this
The problem
#### Outreach tools tell you what happened yesterday.
Context
Sales and outreach work happens between meetings, in transit, in the gaps — but the tooling assumes you are sitting at a desk with a wide screen and an hour to spare.
What kept breaking
Follow-ups were manual and therefore inconsistent. Reporting arrived in batches, so by the time you knew a campaign was underperforming it had already finished sending. And the moment a prospect opened an email — the one moment when a reply actually lands — nobody was watching.
The real requirement
Not a mobile port of a dashboard. A product where the live activity stream is the primary surface, because on a phone the thing worth showing is what is happening right now.
The approach
#### Four flows, designed around the live stream.
The dashboard is a scoreboard, not a spreadsheet. Everything else in the product exists to feed it or to act on what it shows.
01
##### Import
Lead lists pulled directly from Google Drive under OAuth 2.0, so no credentials are handled by the app and no CSV is emailed around.
02
##### Compose
Campaign composition with spin-syntax variation, so every recipient receives a genuinely distinct message rather than an obvious template.
03
##### Track
A live activity feed streaming sends, opens, and clicks across every active campaign simultaneously, with a lifetime scoreboard above it.
04
##### Follow up
Automated sequences triggered by recipient behaviour, plus a manual override to fire an individual targeted message the moment it matters.
Inside the app
#### Screens from the shipped build.
Real screenshots across the full campaign lifecycle — import, compose, send, track, and follow up. Recipient addresses in the tracking feed are blurred for privacy.
Pulse DashboardLifetime scoreboard
Import LeadsGoogle Drive integration
Campaign EditorSmart compose
Auto Follow-upsSequence builder
Deliverability EngineSend-rate control
System MonitorLive send progress
Spy RadarLive tracking stream
Manual StrikePrecision override
Engineering highlights
#### The parts that were harder than they look.
Real-time tracking stream
Open and click events arrive continuously and out of order across multiple concurrent campaigns. Rendering that as a calm, readable feed on a phone screen — rather than a flickering wall of rows — was more of a state-management problem than a display one.
OAuth without credential handling
Google OAuth 2.0 on top of Supabase means the app is granted scoped access rather than ever holding a user's password. Drive import runs through the same grant, so lead lists never leave the user's own Google account boundary before being read.
Deliverability engine
Sending is rate-controlled and paced rather than dumped, and message bodies vary per recipient. Both exist for the same reason: bulk-identical, burst-sent mail is what spam filtering is designed to catch, and reputation is far easier to protect than to repair.
Automation with a manual override
Sequences run on their own, but every automated step can be interrupted by a human acting on a live signal. Full automation is efficient; the reply usually comes from the one message a person chose to send at exactly the right moment.
Scope at a glance
#### What the build actually covers.
10 Designed and built screens across the full campaign lifecycle.
04 Core flows: import, compose, track, and follow up.
2.0 Google OAuth grant scope — no user credentials ever handled by the app.
Live Open and click events streamed to the dashboard as they happen.

#### The stack behind GMassPulse.

## WUM Connect Case Study: University App | AppVion Studio
URL: https://appvionstudio.com/work/wum-connect/
======================================================================

University communication platform
### WUM Connect: one campus announcement that actually reaches everyone.
A role-based university app where administrators, faculty, and students each see a different product built on the same data. Real-time announcements, faculty and student records, results publishing, and push notifications — replacing notice boards, WhatsApp groups, and word of mouth.
Jetpack Compose Firebase Hilt Role-based access Push notifications
3 user roles Real-time announcements Offline-friendly
Published 16 Aug 2026 · Updated 21 Oct 2026
Watch the Demo Build something like this
The problem
#### A campus announcement is only as good as its worst distribution channel.
Context
University information is time-sensitive and role-specific. An exam reschedule matters urgently to one cohort and not at all to another, and it has to arrive before the exam, not after.
What kept breaking
Notices lived on physical boards, in unofficial WhatsApp groups, and in forwarded screenshots. There was no way to tell who had actually been reached, and no way to stop a stale notice circulating for weeks after it was superseded.
The real requirement
A single authoritative source with role-aware delivery — so the university publishes once, the right people are notified, and the current version is the only one visible.
The approach
#### Three roles, one Firestore-backed source of truth.
01
##### Administration
Publish announcements, manage faculty and student records, oversee departments and admissions information, and send targeted notifications.
02
##### Faculty
Read announcements relevant to teaching staff, and publish results for their own students without going through an administrator.
03
##### Students
A single feed of everything that applies to them — announcements, results, departmental information, and admissions detail.
04
##### Shared backend
Firebase Authentication for identity, Firestore for live data, Storage for attachments, and Cloud Messaging for delivery.
Inside the app
#### Screens from the shipped build.
Real screens across all three roles — the administration console, the teaching staff view, and the student hub.

EventsStudent · Register

DepartmentsPublic · Directory
Engineering highlights
#### The parts that were harder than they look.
Role is a data boundary, not a UI toggle
Each role gets its own navigation graph and its own set of screens rather than one screen with hidden buttons. A student's build has no path to an admin action at all, which is a stronger guarantee than a disabled control.
Announcements that arrive
Firestore keeps the feed live for anyone with the app open; Cloud Messaging reaches everyone who does not. Both paths write to the same record, so an announcement cannot exist as a notification without also existing in the feed.
Bulk student migration
Onboarding an existing cohort is the unglamorous part that decides whether a campus app gets used. A dedicated migration flow imports student records in bulk rather than expecting an administrator to type in a year group by hand.
Offline-friendly reading
Firestore's local cache plus DataStore-held preferences mean an announcement already delivered stays readable on a patchy campus connection, rather than showing a blank screen.

## Attendance Management Case Study | AppVion Studio
URL: https://appvionstudio.com/work/attendance-management/
======================================================================

Institutional attendance platform
### Attendance Management: institutional attendance without a biometric machine.
Attendance is marked on the phone already in the room, works with no signal, syncs when the network returns, and leaves an audit trail nobody can quietly edit. Four roles — teacher, head of department, administrator, and student — each with a purpose-built view of the same records.
Jetpack Compose Firebase WorkManager Offline-first Analytics
4 user roles Works offline Append-only audit log
Published 16 Aug 2026 · Updated 21 Oct 2026
Watch the Demo Build something like this
Capture flow Mark now, sync later
01
Marked in class Section roster loaded and stored locally
02
Queued offline No signal required to finish the register
03
Synced & logged Background worker writes and audits the change
The problem
#### Attendance hardware fails in exactly the places attendance matters.
Context
Biometric attendance machines are expensive per room, queue students at the door, and stop working entirely when the power or the network does. Paper registers avoid all of that and create a different problem: nothing is aggregated and nothing is verifiable.
What kept breaking
Registers were transcribed into spreadsheets weeks later, so shortfalls surfaced long after anything could be done. Corrections were made in place with no record of who changed what. And a lecture hall with poor connectivity meant any online-only system simply could not be used.
The real requirement
Capture that never depends on the network, aggregation that is immediate once synced, and a change history that makes a disputed attendance record answerable.
The approach
#### Four roles, one record, offline by default.
01
##### Teacher
Open the section, mark the register, done. The screen is designed for speed in front of a room, and it does not care whether there is signal.
02
##### Head of department
Analytics across sections and cohorts, so a developing attendance problem is visible while the term is still running.
03
##### Administrator
Master student records, section setup, user management, CSV export, and the audit log covering every change made in the system.
04
##### Student
Claim a student identity once, then see an honest personal attendance record rather than finding out at the end of term.
Engineering highlights
#### The parts that were harder than they look.
Offline capture with background sync
Marking is written locally and drained by a WorkManager job when connectivity returns. The teacher never waits on a spinner and never loses a register because a lecture hall has thick walls.
Large-list performance
Institutional rosters are long. Records are paged rather than loaded wholesale, so scrolling a large cohort stays smooth on the mid-range devices staff actually carry.
Append-only audit log
Corrections are legitimate and expected; silent corrections are not. Every administrative change is appended to a log rather than overwriting history, which is what makes a contested record settleable.
Identity claiming
Students authenticate themselves and then claim their institutional student ID, so the roster imported by an administrator and the person holding the phone are linked without an administrator handing out credentials.
Technology
#### The stack behind Attendance Management.
Kotlin Jetpack Compose Material 3 Coroutines & Flow Firebase Auth Cloud Firestore WorkManager DataStore Navigation Compose Paging CSV Export

## Sports Society Events Case Study | AppVion Studio
URL: https://appvionstudio.com/work/sports-society-events/
======================================================================

Events platform
### Sports Society Events: trials, fixtures, and results in one place.
A sports society runs on sign-up sheets, group chats, and a coach's notebook. This replaces all three — event listings with real registration, per-event chat, leaderboards, and performance tracking that follows a participant across the season.
Jetpack Compose Firebase Material 3 Real-time chat Multi-role
3 user roles Live event chat Season leaderboards
Published 16 Aug 2026 · Updated 21 Oct 2026
Build something like this
Event flow Announce to leaderboard
01
Event published Trials and fixtures with full detail
02
Participants register A real roster, not a comment thread
03
Event chat live Scoped to the people actually attending
04
Performance recorded Coach scoring feeds the leaderboard
The problem
#### Nobody knows who is actually turning up.
Context
A society runs trials, fixtures, and training sessions across several sports at once, with a membership that changes every intake and coaches who only see their own group.
What kept breaking
"Interested" in a group chat is not a registration, so numbers were guesswork until the day. Announcements reached whoever happened to be in the right chat. And performance across a season lived in a coach's own notes, so selection decisions were hard to explain.
The real requirement
A registration that means something, a conversation scoped to the people in the event, and a performance record that survives past the end of the fixture.
The approach
#### Three roles built around the event record.
01
##### Participant
Browse and filter events, register, keep a personal list of registrations, join the event chat, and see standing on the leaderboard.
02
##### Coach
See who registered, run the event, and record performance against individual participants so selection has evidence behind it.
03
##### Administrator
Create and manage events across sports, oversee participation, and review performance across the whole society.
04
##### Shared backend
Firebase Authentication for role-gated access and Firestore for events, registrations, chat messages, and performance records.
Engineering highlights
#### The parts that were harder than they look.
Chat scoped to an event
The chat belongs to the event rather than to a permanent group, so it appears with the fixture and stops mattering when the fixture is over. That single scoping choice is what keeps it useful instead of becoming another muted group.
Performance to leaderboard
A coach's score against a participant is the same record the leaderboard reads. There is no separate tally to reconcile, which is how season standings usually drift out of agreement with reality.
Role-gated navigation
Each role enters its own navigation graph after authentication. A participant's build has no route to a coach's scoring screen at all, rather than hiding it behind a disabled control.
Filtering that matches reality
A society member cares about two or three sports, not twenty. Filtering is a first-class part of the event list rather than a secondary screen, because an unfiltered feed is the same as no feed.

Kotlin Jetpack Compose Material 3 Coroutines & Flow Firebase Auth Cloud Firestore Navigation Compose Real-time Chat Role-Based Access

#### How this compares to the rest of the market.
The largest single variable in software pricing is not the app. It is where the engineers sit. The same product specification produces wildly different invoices depending on the team's cost base, and a large part of a Western agency's rate funds sales, account management, and office overhead rather than engineering.

Comparison figures are drawn from published 2026 industry pricing guides, including Netguru, TechAhead, Velvetech, and Pakistan market reports. AppVion's rate sits at the top of the Pakistani market rather than the bottom — the studio competes on judgement, not on being the cheapest bid.
#### What actually moves the number.
Screen count is the weakest predictor of cost. These seven factors decide almost everything:
Number of user roles. One role is a list and a detail screen. Four roles with different permissions is four products sharing a backend. This is the single biggest driver on operational apps.
Whether the data is live. A screen that refreshes on pull is cheap. A screen that updates the moment a driver moves or a job status changes needs realtime infrastructure, conflict handling, and a great deal more testing.
Offline behaviour. Working offline is not a toggle. It means a local database, a sync queue, and a decision about what happens when two people edit the same record on a bad connection. How offline-first apps work.
Integrations. Payments, maps, SMS, calendars, and existing ERP or CRM systems each carry their own edge cases, credentials, and failure states. Three integrations often cost more than ten screens.
Interface ambition. A functional interface and a premium one differ by motion, empty states, loading states, error states, and the hundred small decisions that make an app feel expensive.
Platform count. Android only is the baseline. Adding iOS through Kotlin Multiplatform typically adds 35 to 55 percent rather than doubling the cost, because the business logic is shared and only the interface is rebuilt. What a Kotlin Multiplatform app costs.
How clear the scope is on day one. The most expensive projects are the ones that changed direction in week six. This is why the Clarity Sprint exists.

#### Pricing questions, answered directly.
##### How much does it cost to build a mobile app in 2026?
A production-ready mobile app costs between $12,000 and $35,000 when built by AppVion Studio. The same product costs $40,000 to $100,000 through an Eastern European agency and $100,000 or more through a US agency, because the largest single cost driver in software is where the engineering team sits, not the app itself. Simple apps with a handful of screens and no backend logic can land below $12,000, and multi-role operational platforms with live tracking and payments run to the top of the range.
##### What is the cheapest way to start?
A Product Clarity Sprint, from $1,500 over one to two weeks. It produces a workflow map, a prioritised feature list, a technical direction, and a realistic launch plan. Most cost overruns happen because a build started before anyone agreed what was being built, so the sprint usually saves more than it costs.
##### Why is AppVion cheaper than a US or European agency?
Because the team is in Multan, Pakistan, and the studio is small. There is no account management layer, no sales team, and no city-centre office to fund. Senior engineering rates in Pakistan run $40 to $80 per hour at the top tier compared with $150 to $250 in the United States. AppVion charges a blended $45 to $65 per hour, which is the top of the local market, not the bottom.
##### Is a fixed price or an hourly rate better?
Fixed price, in almost every case. AppVion quotes a fixed figure per engagement after the scope is clear, and delivery runs against milestones. Hourly billing transfers all the estimation risk to the client and rewards a slow team. The exception is open-ended iteration after launch, which is better suited to a monthly retainer.
##### What does the price not include?
Third-party costs that belong to the client and are paid directly: Apple Developer Program at $99 per year, Google Play Console at a one-off $25, and any hosting, database, mapping, SMS, or payment-processor fees. AppVion sets these accounts up in the client's name so the client owns them outright.
##### How much does an app cost to run after launch?
Budget 15 to 25 percent of the original build cost per year for maintenance across the industry. On a $20,000 build that is roughly $3,000 to $5,000 a year for keeping the app current with OS releases, store policy changes, and dependency updates. AppVion's care and iteration retainer starts at $900 per month and covers both maintenance and ongoing feature work.
##### Do you require full payment upfront?
No. Engagements are split across milestones, with a deposit to begin and the remainder released as each milestone is delivered and reviewed. The client sees working software at each stage rather than a status report.
##### Who owns the code and the app?
The client does, in full, on final payment. That includes the source code, the repository, the store listings, the backend accounts, and the design files. AppVion does not retain a licence or hold accounts hostage.

## Android App Development in Kotlin & Compose | AppVion Studio
URL: https://appvionstudio.com/android-app-development.html
======================================================================

Home
Android App Development
Android app development
### Android apps, built natively in Kotlin.
AppVion Studio builds Android products in Kotlin and Jetpack Compose — the operational kind that people open forty times a day and cannot afford to have fail.
Short answer
AppVion Studio is a native Android development studio. Apps are written in Kotlin against the Android SDK with Jetpack Compose interfaces, backed by Room or SQLDelight for offline storage and Supabase, Firebase, or an existing API for data.
A production Android release costs $12,000 to $35,000 and takes 8 to 16 weeks. The studio specialises in operational software — dispatch, approvals, attendance, field service, and internal business tools — rather than consumer social or gaming apps.
Why native
The stack
Architecture
Work
Questions
#### Why native still wins for operational apps.
Cross-platform frameworks are a reasonable answer to a real problem: two platforms, one budget. They are a poor answer when the app is the operational spine of a business.
Field and operations apps live at the edges of the platform. They run in the background, capture photographs on bad connections, hold a GPS lock while the screen is off, queue writes offline, and fire notifications that people act on within seconds. Those are precisely the areas where an abstraction layer leaks — where you spend a week discovering that a plugin does not expose the API you need, and a second week working around it.
Native Kotlin removes that class of problem. When the platform changes, you adapt directly instead of waiting for a framework to catch up.
#### The stack, and why each piece is there.
Kotlin. The official Android language. Null safety and coroutines remove two of the largest historical sources of crashes and callback complexity.
Jetpack Compose. Declarative interfaces as a function of state. Less code, fewer synchronisation bugs, and motion that is cheap enough to actually do well.
Coroutines and Flow. Structured concurrency for network, database, and realtime streams without a thread-management layer of your own.
Room or SQLDelight. A real local database so the app works on a train, in a basement, or on a site with no signal.
Paging 3. Large lists that stay at 60fps on mid-range hardware instead of loading four thousand rows into memory.
Supabase, Firebase, or your API. Backend chosen to fit the product, not to fit a template. Realtime where realtime earns its cost.
WorkManager. Background sync that survives process death, reboots, and aggressive battery optimisation from manufacturers.
#### How the apps are structured.
Every build uses a layered architecture with a single source of truth for each piece of state: an interface layer in Compose, a domain layer holding business rules, and a data layer that owns the network and the local database. The interface never talks to the network directly.
That sounds like ceremony until the second year, when a new requirement arrives and it turns out to be a change in one layer rather than a search across forty files. Most of what makes an app expensive to maintain is decided in the first three weeks of building it.
#### Android work you can actually inspect.
The studio publishes working prototypes rather than testimonials. Each product below can be explored screen by screen on the work page or through the interactive prototypes on the home page.
SnowGrid — enterprise snow-removal operations: live dispatch on a Mapbox map, a dynamic pricing engine, escrow payouts, and separate owner and driver portals.
GMassPulse — cold-email outreach infrastructure with Google Sheets lead import, a campaign editor, and a deliverability throttling engine.
WUM Connect — role-aware university communication on Firebase with offline-first sync across student, faculty, and admin roles.
Attendance Suite — thousands of attendance records browsed smoothly with Paging 3, exceptions surfaced ahead of the routine.
#### Android questions, answered directly.
##### What is native Android app development?
Native Android development means writing the app in Kotlin against Android's own SDK and interface toolkit, rather than through a cross-platform layer that translates to Android at runtime. The app uses platform components directly, so it gets new Android features on the day they ship, behaves the way users expect, and has no translation layer to debug when something goes wrong.
##### Should I build native Android or cross-platform?
Build native Android when the app is Android-first, leans on device capability such as camera, location, background work, or notifications, or must feel indistinguishable from a first-party app. Choose cross-platform when you need iOS and Android simultaneously on one budget and the app is largely screens over an API. Kotlin Multiplatform is a middle path: shared business logic with a genuinely native interface on each platform.
##### What is Jetpack Compose?
Jetpack Compose is Google's modern declarative UI toolkit for Android, and it is now the default way Android interfaces are written. Instead of describing screens in XML layouts and mutating them from code, the interface is a function of state. In practice it means less code, fewer state-synchronisation bugs, and animation and theming that are far cheaper to build well.
##### How long does an Android app take to build?
A focused first release takes 8 to 12 weeks from a clear scope. A multi-role operational platform with realtime data and payments takes 12 to 16 weeks. A one to two week Product Clarity Sprint before the build is what makes those numbers reliable rather than optimistic.
##### Do you publish the app to Google Play for us?
Yes. The Play Console account is registered in the client's name, and AppVion handles the build signing, store listing, content rating, data safety declarations, and staged rollout. The client owns the listing and the app from day one.
##### What Android versions do you support?
Typically the current Android release back four or five versions, which covers the overwhelming majority of active devices. The exact floor is a business decision made during scoping, because supporting older versions costs testing time that may be better spent elsewhere.
##### Can you take over an existing Android app?
Yes. That usually starts with an architecture and code review to establish what is salvageable, followed by a staged plan so the app keeps shipping while it is modernised. A full stop-and-rewrite is rarely the right answer for a product with live users.

## Kotlin Multiplatform Development Services | AppVion Studio
URL: https://appvionstudio.com/services/kotlin-multiplatform-development/
======================================================================

Kotlin Multiplatform development
### Kotlin Multiplatform development: share the logic, keep the interface native.
One Kotlin module holds your domain models, business rules, networking, and local storage. Android and iOS each keep a genuinely native interface on top. You stop maintaining the same pricing rule in two languages, and your users never feel like they are using a port.
Book a 20-min App Strategy Session See a KMP build in detail
The actual argument
#### The bug you cannot afford is the one that exists on only one platform.
Cross-platform frameworks are usually sold on cost. That is the least interesting benefit. The real one is consistency: when a fare calculation, an order state machine, or a permission rule exists once instead of twice, it cannot silently disagree with itself between your Android and iOS users.
##### Rules cannot drift
Pricing, validation, and state transitions live in one place. A fix applies everywhere at once, rather than being ported and half-remembered three months later.
##### The interface stays native
Jetpack Compose on Android, SwiftUI on iOS. Platform conventions, gestures, accessibility, and performance are real rather than approximated by a rendering layer.
##### Incremental adoption
KMP does not demand a rewrite. A well-layered Android app can move its domain and data layers into a shared module while the existing interface keeps working. How a migration runs.
##### No framework lock-in tax
Shared code is plain Kotlin. If a platform ever needs to diverge, it diverges at the interface layer without unpicking a proprietary runtime.
What we share, and what we do not
#### The split that keeps KMP projects healthy.
Sharing too much is how multiplatform projects turn brittle. The boundary matters more than the technology.
Shared
Domain models and business rules
Use cases and validation logic
Networking and API contracts
Local database and caching
Repository and data-source layers
Dependency injection wiring
Platform-specific
All user interface code
Navigation and lifecycle handling
Permissions and system dialogs
Camera, location, and sensors
Push notification handling
Secure credential storage
Why the line sits there
Business logic is where correctness lives and where duplication is genuinely dangerous. Interface and platform integration are where users notice compromise immediately. Sharing the first and never the second gives you consistency without the uncanny feel of a ported app.
Technology
#### The KMP stack we work in.
Kotlin Multiplatform Jetpack Compose Compose Multiplatform Coroutines & Flow Ktor Client SQLDelight Koin kotlinx.serialization kotlinx-datetime Supabase Firebase SQLCipher

This is not a first experiment with the technology. Both platforms below run shared Kotlin in production code.

FAQ
#### Kotlin Multiplatform questions we get asked.
How is KMP different from Flutter or React Native?
Flutter and React Native share the user interface and render it themselves. Kotlin Multiplatform shares the logic — domain models, business rules, networking, local storage — while each platform keeps its own genuinely native interface. The result feels native because it is native, and the rules that matter cannot drift between your Android and iOS users. We go through this in depth, including where each option breaks, in Kotlin Multiplatform vs React Native for business apps and Kotlin Multiplatform vs Flutter.
Is Kotlin Multiplatform production ready?
Yes. KMP is stable and used in production by major engineering teams. We have shipped multi-app KMP platforms including a three-app logistics system with realtime dispatch, payments, and offline-first sync.
Can you migrate our existing Android app to KMP?
Usually yes, and incrementally rather than as a rewrite. A well-structured Android app already separates its domain and data layers; those move into a shared module first while the Android interface keeps working untouched, and an iOS interface is added afterwards.
When is KMP the wrong choice?
When you only need one platform and have no near-term plan for the second, KMP adds structure you are not yet using. It is also a poor fit for products that are mostly interface with very little business logic, since there is little worth sharing. In both cases we will tell you to build native for one platform instead.
Start the conversation
#### Considering Kotlin Multiplatform for your product?
Bring the product, the platforms you need, and the constraints. If KMP is the wrong tool for it, that is a useful answer to get early — and you will get it straight.
Book a 20-min App Strategy Session WhatsApp us

## Move an Android App to Kotlin Multiplatform | AppVion Studio
URL: https://appvionstudio.com/services/android-to-kotlin-multiplatform/
======================================================================

Kotlin Multiplatform migration
### Add iOS to your Android app without starting again.
If your Android app is written in Kotlin, most of what makes it valuable can be shared with iOS: the business rules, the data layer, the networking and the offline storage. We move those into a shared Kotlin module step by step, keep your Android app shipping the whole time, and build the iOS app on the same core.
Book a free 20-min call How we do Kotlin Multiplatform
How the move runs
#### Five steps, and the Android app never stops.
##### 1. Map the layers
In the Clarity Sprint we read the codebase, mark what is domain, data and interface, and find the code that has to be untangled first.
##### 2. Share the core
Domain models, rules, validation, networking and local storage move into a shared Kotlin module, one feature at a time.
##### 3. Keep Android shipping
The Android interface stays as it is and keeps releasing on top of the shared module throughout.
##### 4. Build iOS on the same core
The iOS app gets its interface, native SwiftUI or shared Compose Multiplatform, and calls the same rules as Android.
##### 5. Release both
From here a rule is written and fixed once, and both apps get it in the same release.
What moves and what stays
#### The boundary that keeps a migration safe.
Business logic is where correctness lives and where duplication is dangerous. Interface and platform integration are where users notice compromise. We share the first and keep the second platform-specific.
##### Moves to shared Kotlin
Domain models and business rules; use cases and validation; networking and API contracts; local database and caching; repositories and dependency injection.
##### Stays on each platform
Interface code (unless you choose Compose Multiplatform); navigation and lifecycle; permissions and system dialogs; camera, location and sensors; push notifications; secure credential storage.
##### Signs you are ready
Kotlin code, business rules kept out of Activities and Fragments, and a repository or data layer. Missing pieces are fixed first, inside the plan.
Proof

Logistics platform

Three apps from one shared Kotlin codebase: customer, rider and admin control tower. The customer app is live on Google Play.

FAQ
#### Questions people ask first.
Do we need to rewrite the Android app?
Usually not. A well-structured Android app already separates its domain and data layers. Those move into a shared Kotlin module while the Android interface keeps working untouched.
Will our Android users notice anything?
They should not. The Android app keeps its own interface and keeps shipping while the shared module is introduced underneath it.
Do we need iOS developers?
The iOS app needs an interface: native SwiftUI on top of the shared module, or Compose Multiplatform screens shared with Android. We build either and tell you which suits your product.
How long does it take and what does it cost?
It depends on how cleanly the app is layered today, which is exactly what the Clarity Sprint (from $1,500, one to two weeks) establishes. You get a fixed quote and timeline before any build starts; full builds run $12,000 to $35,000.

Field service app development
### Field service apps for crews, dispatchers and the customers they serve.
Jobs that live in phone calls, quotes that are guessed, and "it's done" with no proof: we replace that with one system where the office, the crew and the customer read the same job. Built from two field products we have shipped, SnowGrid and PropFix.
Book a free 20-min call See SnowGrid
What breaks without a system
#### Field work is coordinated by whoever keeps chasing it.
##### Dispatch by phone
Work goes to whoever answers first, not whoever is nearest or free.
##### Quotes by guesswork
When nobody measures the job, margin swings from job to job.
##### "Done" is a claim
Without before and after evidence on the job record, every disputed invoice is one word against another.
##### Nothing is searchable
Open jobs, owed payments and history live in messages and memory.
What we build
#### The parts every field service app needs.
##### Jobs and work orders
Raise a job against a property or site, assign it, and watch its status move without calling anyone.
##### Dispatch
Assign by who is nearest and free, with live positions on a map when the work needs it.
##### Proof of work
Before and after photos attached to the job itself, so the evidence is on the record months later.
##### Quotes from measurement
Measure an area on a satellite map and price it from the company's own rates.
##### Offline-first
Crews keep working without signal; the app syncs later and says when it last did. How offline-first works.
##### Roles and payments
Office, crew and customer each get their own app view, with payouts and escrow where money is involved.

## Delivery & Courier App Development | AppVion Studio
URL: https://appvionstudio.com/delivery-app-development/
======================================================================

Delivery and courier app development
### Delivery apps where every parcel leaves evidence.
Customer booking, rider dispatch, live tracking and cash-on-delivery that reconciles against the platform's own ledger. Built from D. Delivery, our three-app Kotlin Multiplatform courier platform, whose customer app is live on Google Play.
Get D. Delivery on Google Play Read the D. Delivery case study
The real problem
#### Courier disputes are won by whoever has evidence.
In D. Delivery the goods were phones, laptops and electronics, where one disputed parcel can cost more than a month of delivery revenue. Bookings ran on WhatsApp, cash was reconciled by hand, and riders were assigned by whoever answered first.
##### No record of condition
Nobody could prove what state a device was in at pickup.
##### Cash that never matched
Cash on delivery was reconciled by hand at the end of the day.
##### Dispatch by phone
The first rider to answer got the job, not the nearest one.
##### Customers calling for status
There was nothing for them to look at.
What we build
#### Three apps, one source of truth.
##### Customer app
Booking with address search, insurance based on declared value, live tracking with a traffic-aware ETA, receipt and rating.
##### Rider app
Job alerts, guided pickup and drop-off, dual video proof, recipient e-signature, wallet and earnings, offline-first sync.
##### Admin control tower
Manual dispatch, rider approval and documents, pricing, dispute flags and end-of-day cash settlement against the ledger.
##### Expanding-radius dispatch
New orders search a small radius first and widen step by step until a rider accepts, with the admin alerted if nobody does.
##### Evidence pipeline
Videos and signatures are compressed on the phone and stored per order; uploads queue in the background on weak signal.
##### Money on the record
Cash on delivery is settled against the platform's own ledger, not the rider's word.

FAQ
#### Questions people ask first.
Do you build the rider app and the admin panel too?
Yes. A delivery business needs three products: a customer booking app, a rider job app and an admin control tower. In D. Delivery all three share one Kotlin codebase and one database.
How does proof of delivery work?
The rider records a video at pickup and at drop-off, and the recipient signs on the phone. The evidence is compressed on the device and stored under the order, so it holds up in a dispute.
Can riders keep working on a weak signal?
Yes. Uploads are queued by a background worker, so a rider is never blocked from finishing a job by the network.
What does a delivery app cost?
A multi-app delivery platform sits in the $20,000 to $35,000 range over 12 to 16 weeks. A focused first release is $12,000 to $18,000. Most projects start with a $1,500 Clarity Sprint that ends in a fixed quote.
